title: Fair shares
goal: I can name fractions of a whole. I can compare fractions and add like fractions. I can solve fair-sharing stories with a bar.

learn.intro: A fraction names equal parts of one whole. The bottom number says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The top number says how many parts we take.

example.problem: Kumar cuts a pizza into 8 equal slices. He eats 3 slices. What fraction did he eat? What fraction is left?
steps: The slices are equal. There are 8 of them: the bottom number is 8.
He eats 3 slices: the top number is 3. He ate 3/8.

howto.title: How to name a fraction
steps: Check that the parts are equal.
Count all the parts: the bottom number.
Count the parts you take: the top number.
Same bottom number? Just add or subtract the tops.

facts.title: Remember
lines: More parts means smaller parts: 1/6 is less than 1/4.
Like fractions: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. The bottom number stays.

try.text: Mei cuts a cake into 10 equal slices and eats 3. The part of the cake left is {b}
try.explanation: 10 - 3 = 7 slices are left. Each slice is 1/10, so 7/10 is left. Check: 3/10 + 7/10 = 10/10 = 1 whole.

items.text: Each shape is cut into 4 parts. Is each shape cut into quarters (4 EQUAL parts)?
items.explanation: Quarters must be 4 parts of the SAME size. A, C and E are quarters. In B and F one part is much greater than the other three. In D the parts are not the same size. In E the four triangles are all the same size.

items.text: Write the shaded fraction. Write the fraction not shaded.

parts.label: d
parts.text: To make 8/12 shaded in C, shade {b} more parts.

items.explanation: The bottom number is how many equal parts there are. (a) A has 5 parts and 2 are shaded: 2/5 shaded, 3/5 not shaded. (b) B has 8 parts, 6 shaded: 6/8 and 2/8. (c) C has 12 parts, 5 shaded: 5/12 and 7/12. (d) 8/12 means 8 parts shaded. 5 are shaded, so 8 - 5 = 3 more.

items.text: The whole is 1. Fill in the missing number.
items.explanation: (a) 6 sixths make 1 whole. (b) 1 whole cut into 9 equal parts is 9/9. (c) 1 whole is 8/8, and 8 - 4 = 4, so 4/8 + 4/8 = 1.

items.text: The fraction wall shows bars of the same length. One part of each bar is shaded.
items.explanation: The more parts a bar is cut into, the smaller each part. (a) Thirds are greater than quarters. (b) Eighths are smaller than sixths. (c) Order: 1/8, 1/6, 1/4, 1/2.

items.text: The same bottom number means the same size parts. Circle the greater fraction.
items.explanation: When the bottom numbers are the same, the parts are the same size, so more parts is greater. (a) 6/10 is greater than 3/10. (b) 7/12 is greater than 5/12. (c) 2/7, 4/7, 6/7.

items.text: Add or take away. The bottom number stays the same.
items.explanation: (a) 3 twelfths + 6 twelfths = 9 twelfths. (b) 7 eighths - 2 eighths = 5 eighths. (c) 1 whole is 5/5, and 5/5 - 3/5 = 2/5. (d) 1 whole is 9/9, and 9/9 - 4/9 = 5/9.

items.text: A pizza is cut into 10 equal slices. Siti eats the slices marked S. Ravi eats the slices marked R.

parts.label: a
parts.text: They eat {b} of the pizza altogether.

items.explanation: Siti ate 3 slices and Ravi ate 4 slices. (a) 3/10 + 4/10 = 7/10. (b) 10/10 - 7/10 = 3/10. (c) 4 is more than 3, so Ravi. (d) 4/10 - 3/10 = 1/10.

items.text: A cake is shared equally among 5 children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each child gets {b} of the cake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Kumar and Mei are 2 of the children. Together they get {b}.

items.explanation: (a) 5 equal shares: each is 1/5. (b) 1/5 + 1/5 = 2/5. (c) The whole is 5/5. 5/5 - 2/5 = 3/5.

items.text: The number line goes from 0 to 1. It is cut into 8 equal steps.
items.explanation: Each step is 1/8. (a) A is 3 steps from 0: 3/8. (b) B is 7 steps from 0: 7/8.

items.text: Ravi and Siti each have a pizza of the same size. Ravi eats 3/4 of his pizza. Siti eats 5/8 of hers.
items.explanation: The bars are the same length. 3/4 of the first bar covers 6 of the small eighths, because each quarter is 2 eighths. Siti eats 5 eighths. Ravi eats 6 eighths, so Ravi eats 1/8 more.
items.hint: Line up the bars. Cut each quarter in 2 equal parts.

items.text: Mei eats 1/4 of a pizza. Then Ali eats half of what is left.
items.explanation: (a) 1/4 eaten, so 3/4 is left. On the bar of 8 parts, 1/4 is 2 parts, and 6 parts are left. (b) Half of 6 parts is 3 parts: Ali eats 3/8. (c) 6 - 3 = 3 parts are left: 3/8.
items.hint: Cut each part in 2 equal parts to make eighths.

items.text: Two fractions have the bottom number 12. Together they make 1 whole. The greater one is 6/12 more.
items.explanation: The whole is 12/12. Take away the extra 6/12: 6/12 is left. Share it between the two equal parts: 3/12 and 3/12. Give the extra back to one of them: 3/12 and 9/12. Check: 3/12 + 9/12 = 12/12.
items.hint: Take away the extra 6/12. Share what is left.

items.text: Beyond: equal fractions. Different fractions can cover the same length. 1/2 and 2/4 and 4/8 are equal.
items.explanation: (a) A half of 6 sixths is 3 sixths. (b) A third is 2 sixths, so 2 thirds are 4 sixths. (c) A quarter is 2 eighths, so 3 quarters are 6 eighths.
items.hint: Line up 2 bars of the same length. Cut one into more parts.

items.text: Nine equal pieces of cake are shared by 3 children. The shares must all be different. Each share is 1 piece or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many different ways are there? {b}

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the way where the greatest share is 6/9, the other shares are {b}/9 and {b}/9.

items.explanation: The 3 different numbers of pieces add to 9. With 1 piece for the smallest: 1 + 2 + 6 and 1 + 3 + 5. With 2 pieces: 2 + 3 + 4. 1 + 4 + 4 repeats a number. So 3 ways. The way with 6/9 is 1/9, 2/9 and 6/9.
items.hint: Start with the smallest share, 1 piece. Then try 2.

items.text: Make your own fair-share story. Picture a cake with 8 equal pieces. Three people eat different shares and some is left. Write each share as a fraction. Many answers are right.

answer.text: Open. Example: Ali eats 3/8, Mei eats 2/8, Ben eats 1/8 and 2/8 is left. 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8 eighths = 1 whole.

items.explanation: A good story has shares and leftovers that add to 8/8. Example: 3/8 + 2/8 + 1/8 + 2/8 = 8/8 = 1 whole.
items.hint: Add all the shares and what is left. Do you get 8/8?

rows: Check: shares and what is left make 1 whole:

items.text: My top number is 1. I am less than 1/3 and more than 1/9. Which fractions fit? Find ALL of them.
items.explanation: With 1 on top, the greater the bottom number, the smaller the fraction. 1/3 is too big and 1/9 is too small. 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/7 and 1/8 are in between: 5 answers.
items.hint: Greater bottom number, smaller part. Try 1/4, 1/5 ...

items.text: What fraction is shaded? {b}
items.explanation: The bar has 8 equal parts. 5 are shaded. The fraction is 5/8.

items.text: Which is greater?   {circ:1/5|1/9}
items.explanation: The more parts a whole is cut into, the smaller each part. 5 parts are greater than 9 parts, so 1/5 is greater.
2 sevenths + 4 sevenths = 6 sevenths. The bottom number stays 7.

items.text: A pizza has 12 slices. Ali eats 5/12 and Mei eats 3/12. How much is left? {b}
